Self-healing materials

By: Eugene Botha | Production

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
a new generation of materials that have the ability to heal themselves if cracked or broken

Summary:
Scientists have developed aircraft wings that can detect and repair small-scale damage to their structure. Modern aircraft are made with carbon fibre-reinforced composites. These are high performance, lightweight and stiff making them an ideal material for aeroplanes or wind turbines. However, damage to the composite structure can be difficult to detect. The researchers added microcapsules to the composite. If the aircraft wing is damaged these microcapsules rupture and come into contact with a catalyst. A chemical reaction takes place which causes hardening (polymerisation) to 'glue' together any cracks. The Wass Research Group says that this can give up to 100 per cent recovery of mechanical strength.Professor Wass was interviewed in an exclusive by the Independent on Sunday. In the interview he said he expected self-healing products to reach consumers in the “very near future” and said that inspiration came from the body's ability to heal itself by forming scabs.

Further information:
BRISTOL has long been at the centre research into the ground-breaking materials that are being used to build the aeroplanes of the future. The work taking place at the National Composite Centre is leading the world and changing the face of the aviation industry.

But now a team of scientists from Bristol University has gone one step further and come up with a miraculous compound that can actually heal itself.

And if the new technology works not only will it help improve safety in aviation it could also be used in hundreds of different products from nail varnish to safety helmets.

The principles are based along the same lines as the way the human body heals itself through blood clotting.

The research is being unveiled for the first time at a Royal Society Meeting in London and has already been hailed as a major step forward for manufacturing.

The team's ground-breaking work started "on the back of an envelope" but has now got to the stage where it has become usable technology.

As well as working for aeroplane fuselages it could also be used to improve nail polish, golf clubs, tennis racquets, fishing rods, bike helmets and even cracked mobile phone screens.

The cosmetics giant L'Oréal has contacted the scientists to register its interest.

The team has been working on the project for the last three years and even they say it is close to science fiction. The work is so far advanced that the team has been able to produce a set of wings.

Professor Duncan Wass, who is leading the research, said there are high hopes that airlines will be able to purchase self-healing products in the 'very near future'.

The researchers have been working with aerospace engineers in nearby Filton to look at ways to prevent tiny cracks forming in an aircraft's wings and fuselage.

Professor Wass said: "We took inspiration from the human body. We have not evolved to withstand any damage – if we were like that we would have a skin as thick as a rhinoceros – but if we do get damaged, we bleed, and it scabs and heals.

"We just put that same sort of function into a synthetic material: let's have something that can heal itself."

He added: "We are definitely getting to the stage where in the next five or 10 years we are going to see things like mobile phone screens that can heal themselves if they crack."

The healing material can take anywhere between a couple of hours and a day to recover with the process taking place faster in warmer climates.

The research is being presented for the first time in public at a conference called Catalysis Improving Society.

Professor Wass said: "We are definitely getting to the stage where in the next five or 10 years we're going to see things like mobile phone screens that can heal themselves if they crack."

Self-healing technology first emerged in 2001, when researchers at the University of Illinois in the US created a plastic which could repair itself.

The same team followed that up in 2014 by creating a polymer which could fix holes of up to three centimetres.

As well as help to save lives the technology will also help make safety checks by airlines become much cheaper to carry out.

Airbus had to pay out billions when its superjumbo the A380 developed tiny cracks in its wings three years ago.

The problem eventually cost the plane manufacturer £120 million to correct.

Scientists have developed aircraft wings that can detect and repair small-scale damage to their structure. Professor Duncan Wass, from Bristol University, presented the research, funded by the Engineering and Physical Sciences Research Council (EPSRC), at a scientific meeting organised by the UK's Catalysis Hub. The event at the Royal Society highlighted the latest research into catalysis and how it can improve society with applications for energy and the environment. The UK's Catalysis Hub is funded by EPSRC with catalysis science supporting UK economic growth.

How the technology works:
Modern aircraft are made with carbon fibre-reinforced composites. These are high performance, lightweight and stiff making them an ideal material for aeroplanes or wind turbines. However, damage to the composite structure can be difficult to detect. The researchers added microcapsules to the composite. If the aircraft wing is damaged these microcapsules rupture and come into contact with a catalyst. A chemical reaction takes place which causes hardening (polymerisation) to 'glue' together any cracks. The Wass Research Group says that this can give up to 100 per cent recovery of mechanical strength.Professor Wass was interviewed in an exclusive by the Independent on Sunday. In the interview he said he expected self-healing products to reach consumers in the “very near future” and said that inspiration came from the body's ability to heal itself by forming scabs.

Prof Duncan Wass writes:
Fibre-reinforced composites are the modern materials of choice where high performance must be combined with low weight, such as aerospace structures (aeroplanes, wind turbines). However, impact damage to composite structures can be difficult to detect but result in a drastic reduction in mechanical properties. We are adopting a bio-inspired approach to effect damage detection and self-healing.

This is a collaborative area of research with Ian Bond and Richard Trask in the Department of Aerospace Engineering, within the ACCIS composites research group. We are providing novel damage detection and self-healing chemistries, to combine with their ability to manufacture and incorporate multifunctional hollow fibres, microcapsules and vascular networks within both composite laminates and sandwich structures. The essential chemistry relies on catalysts which are ‘triggered’ by damage events to cause the polymerisation of a reservoir of monomer held within the composite structure.

Script:


LINK CLAIRE MAWISA:
That was one of modern life’s little disasters. That very crucial part of all our lives damaged beyond repair.
V/O:
But wouldn’t it be marvellous if somehow the damage to the screen could be instantly undone.

Impossible? //These two scientists from Bristol in the UK say the day when your cell phone will repair itself, is not far off.
Duncan
It sounds impossible. It sounds like science fiction and it sounds like there’s no way we could achieve this. And yet if we think about the problem more deaply, maybe we can achive something that sounds impossible.
V/O:
And these two men are doing just that – working on the impossible. Duncan Wass is a professor in Chemistry and Ian Bond is professor in Aerospace Engineering. Together they are creating materials of the future, or perhaps of science fiction – materials that can repair themselves.

Their main focus is on creating airplane wings that can self-heal when damaged or structures on the space station that can automatically repair themselves. But that is not all.
Ian:
And then there is the more mundane products as well. Sporting goods. Those kind of things. Where people would like to prolong the life or give it more robustness, so you dropped your tennis racquet, it cracked or was damaged and can repair itself. And then there’s the really, really mundane. You know the mobile phone screen repair after you have dropped it. Can you have a mobile phone screen that repairs itself miraculously after you’ve dropped it?
V/O:
At the University of Bristol Duncan and Ian’s collaboration is creating remarkable new materials.
Duncan:
Our specific interest is in carbon fibre composite materials. So these composite materials are the sorts of materials that are now used for making things like wind turbines. Increasingly they are used in automotive for cars as well. They are also used for sports equipment. Many people might have carbon fibre fishing rods or tennis rackets, golf clubs.
V/O:
And, very significantly, more and more composite materials are used in the aerospace field.
Duncan:
Traditionally aeroplanes were made out of metal, aluminium in particular, a lighter metal. More recently though composite materials are replacing those traditional metals. And most of the modern generation airliners, things like the Airbus A380, Boeing 787, a large part of those aeroplanes will be made out of composite materials because they are very stiff they are strong but much lighter compared to the metal materials that we used in the past.
LINK:
But this new generation of materials also have shortcomings. Although they are very strong and light, they are also brittle and under severe stress they can develop tiny cracks.
V/O:
And this is especially worrying for aircraft.
Ian:
In an aeroplane you get hit by hailstone or debris off the runway. The damage is not sufficient to visibly damage the aircraft, but there could be enough damage in the structure that over a period of time that damage could propagate and become much more of a serious issue.
V/O:
For example when moisture or water gets into these tiny cracks and freezes, it expands and the crack grows bigger and bigger. Unaddressed, this could eventually lead to structural failure and disaster. But initially these tiny cracks are not visible at all. Duncan and Ian decided to hone in on this problem.
Duncan:
So if we can repair those micro-cracks we go a long way to making the structure much more robust.
LINK:
To find a way to repair these micro-cracks Ian and Duncan started to think out of the box.
Ian:
So the analogy really is the human body . We all do self-healing without thinking about it. And it’s really, can we take that idea and put it into an engineering artefact that can then do the same thing. Particularly where you’ve got the safety critical systems, so the obvious thing is in an aeroplane.
V/O:
When a blood vessel is damaged tiny cells in the blood called platelets bind together at the wound site where chemical reactions form a clot and seal the wound so it can heal. Duncan and Ian decided to look at a way to simulate what happens in the human body.

They knew they needed hollow structures and special chemical compounds to achieve a similar effect.
LINK:
And this where their skills complement each other: Ian could create all kind of composite structures with carbon fibres and Duncan could develop a range of fluids to put into these hollow fibres.
V/O:
And this is exactly what they did. Ian engineered microscopic hollow spheres like these. They are called micro-capsules.
Duncan:
If you were to look at these; it just looks like a white powder. Actually these spheres you’d get several of them across a human hair, they’re so small. You can barely see individual ones with the human eye.
V/O:
Duncan then developed two different liquid fillings for the micro capsules. When these liquids come into contact with each other, the blend hardens instantly. Billions of these filled microcapsules can then be embedded into composite materials in the manufacturing process.
Duncan:
If these spilt open there is a crack that comes open from the material that burst these micro-capsules. The liquid agent can them come out of that.
V/O:
Then, when the liquids leak from the broken capsules, they come into contact with each other and start to set immediately.
Duncan:
And then it will glue any cracks that we have back together. So this is liquid when it is in the capsule but when it hardens, when it heals, it looks very much the same on a chemical level as the material that was already there in the composite structure. And this is why it heals so well or one of the reasons anyway.
LINK:
So, with this method tiny cracks in composite materials are healed before they can grow bigger and weaken a whole structure.
V/O:
And this is of course of great interest to aircraft manufacturers and space agencies.

But outside the area of aerospace the idea of materials that can repair themselves is also taking the scientific world by storm.
Ian:
A number of people around the world. Primarily in the US began looking at the idea of self-healing to effect repairs. And that’s where it began. It was the use of hollow fibres. It evolved from there and we’re now looking at micro capsules, we’re now looking at fully vascular systems.
V/O:
Self-healing paints and coatings are already used by some car manufacturers. They allow small scratches to self-heal when heat is applied.

And self-healing nail polish is on the horizon.

NASA has developed special glass that repairs itself after a bullet passes through it. This will one day make the International Space Station that’s constantly bombarded by objects travelling at high velocity - that much safer.

Concrete is a great building material but inevitably it starts to crack. Now a scientist in the Netherlands has started to mix limestone producing bacteria into the concrete. These bacteria can lie dormant for up to 200 years. Then when the concrete cracks and water seeps in, they start to produce limestone, and any cracks in the concrete are patched over.
LINK:
Ian and Duncan’s work is focused on compound structure used in aeroplanes. However, they do not foresee that whole planes will be built from their material.
Ian:
There are clearly areas on an aeroplane for instance where you know you are going to get damage. The underneath of wings, the wheels, debris thrown up from on the runway, the leading edges of the plane where you flying through the air, the nose cone. And there is not really a need to have it everywhere. Doors and hatches as well. They get banged quite a lot with loading and unloading. So there are clearly areas that you would target.
V/O:
After their microcapsules have healed a crack, Ian and Duncan’s test results indicate that they achieve a 100 per cent recovery of mechanical strength.
Duncan:
For some of the materials we have a 100% in lab conditions which is very encouraging. It surprised us how well these work. We have to put a note of caution here of course this is in lab conditions and I think in real life applications there are many more tests that we need to do to really understand exactly how well they would heal in those. But certainly a hundred percent with the tests we have done so far is very encouraging.
LINK:
However, their ultimate goal is materials that can self-heal repeatedly.
Duncan:
What would be great thought would be like the human body, that we can not only repair ourselves wounds, but again and again and again. So this is where we need a vascular system to do this. If we have a vascular system them we can have a series of veins through the structure with a liquid healing agent in those and we can basically pump as much healing agent as we need to, time and time again into damaged regions.
V/O:
This has just been achieved in the USA. Scientists have managed to repair larger holes in structures through a vascular system. The material has tiny veins like the human body. When damage occurs, two solutions are pumped to the area where they mix and self-repair the hole.
LINK:
Being involved in such ground-breaking technology is for Duncan literally like living in a science fiction dream world where the possibilities are endless.
Duncan:
I admit that I quite like watching a bit of science fiction and think ‘Well how could you do this for real?’ It seems impossible some of the things they say in science fiction. And yet there are many examples now where people have been inspired and think, well how can we do this for real? And I think self healing technology is maybe a good example of something which seems like science fiction but in fact now it’s becoming science fact.

V/O: When a blood vessel is damaged tiny cells in the blood called platelets bind together at the wound site where chemical reactions form a clot and seal the wound so it can heal. Duncan and Ian decided to look at a way to simulate what happens in the human body. They knew they needed hollow structures and special chemical compounds to achieve a similar effect. LINK: And this where their skills complement each other: Ian could create all kind of composite structures with carbon fibres and Duncan could develop a range of fluids to put into these hollow fibres. V/O: And this is exactly what they did. Ian engineered microscopic hollow spheres like these. They are called micro-capsules. Duncan: If you were to look at these; it just looks like a white powder. Actually these spheres you’d get several of them across a human hair, they’re so small. You can barely see individual ones with the human eye. V/O: Duncan then developed two different liquid fillings for the micro capsules. When these liquids come into contact with each other, the blend hardens instantly. Billions of these filled microcapsules can then be embedded into composite materials in the manufacturing process. Duncan: If these spilt open there is a crack that comes open from the material that burst these micro-capsules. The liquid agent can them come out of that. V/O: Then, when the liquids leak from the broken capsules, they come into contact with each other and start to set immediately. Duncan: And then it will glue any cracks that we have back together. So this is liquid when it is in the capsule but when it hardens, when it heals, it looks very much the same on a chemical level as the material that was already there in the composite structure. And this is why it heals so well or one of the reasons anyway. LINK: So, with this method tiny cracks in composite materials are healed before they can grow bigger and weaken a whole structure. V/O: And this is of course of great interest to aircraft manufacturers and space agencies. But outside the area of aerospace the idea of materials that can repair themselves is also taking the scientific world by storm. Ian: A number of people around the world. Primarily in the US began looking at the idea of self-healing to effect repairs. And that’s where it began. It was the use of hollow fibres. It evolved from there and we’re now looking at micro capsules, we’re now looking at fully vascular systems. V/O: Self-healing paints and coatings are already used by some car manufacturers. They allow small scratches to self-heal when heat is applied. And self-healing nail polish is on the horizon. NASA has developed special glass that repairs itself after a bullet passes through it. This will one day make the International Space Station that’s constantly bombarded by objects travelling at high velocity - that much safer. Concrete is a great building material but inevitably it starts to crack. Now a scientist in the Netherlands has started to mix limestone producing bacteria into the concrete. These bacteria can lie dormant for up to 200 years. Then when the concrete cracks and water seeps in, they start to produce limestone, and any cracks in the concrete are patched over. LINK: Ian and Duncan’s work is focused on compound structure used in aeroplanes. However, they do not foresee that whole planes will be built from their material. Ian: There are clearly areas on an aeroplane for instance where you know you are going to get damage. The underneath of wings, the wheels, debris thrown up from on the runway, the leading edges of the plane where you flying through the air, the nose cone. And there is not really a need to have it everywhere. Doors and hatches as well. They get banged quite a lot with loading and unloading. So there are clearly areas that you would target. V/O: After their microcapsules have healed a crack, Ian and Duncan’s test results indicate that they achieve a 100 per cent recovery of mechanical strength. Duncan: For some of the materials we have a 100% in lab conditions which is very encouraging. It surprised us how well these work. We have to put a note of caution here of course this is in lab conditions and I think in real life applications there are many more tests that we need to do to really understand exactly how well they would heal in those. But certainly a hundred percent with the tests we have done so far is very encouraging. LINK: However, their ultimate goal is materials that can self-heal repeatedly. Duncan: What would be great thought would be like the human body, that we can not only repair ourselves wounds, but again and again and again. So this is where we need a vascular system to do this. If we have a vascular system them we can have a series of veins through the structure with a liquid healing agent in those and we can basically pump as much healing agent as we need to, time and time again into damaged regions. V/O: This has just been achieved in the USA. Scientists have managed to repair larger holes in structures through a vascular system. The material has tiny veins like the human body. When damage occurs, two solutions are pumped to the area where they mix and self-repair the hole. LINK: Being involved in such ground-breaking technology is for Duncan literally like living in a science fiction dream world where the possibilities are endless. Duncan: I admit that I quite like watching a bit of science fiction and think ‘Well how could you do this for real?’ It seems impossible some of the things they say in science fiction. And yet there are many examples now where people have been inspired and think, well how can we do this for real? And I think self healing technology is maybe a good example of something which seems like science fiction but in fact now it’s becoming science fact. metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): a new generation of materials that have the ability to heal themselves if cracked or broken
metadata.Summary: Scientists have developed aircraft wings that can detect and repair small-scale damage to their structure. Modern aircraft are made with carbon fibre-reinforced composites. These are high performance, lightweight and stiff making them an ideal material for aeroplanes or wind turbines. However, damage to the composite structure can be difficult to detect. The researchers added microcapsules to the composite. If the aircraft wing is damaged these microcapsules rupture and come into contact with a catalyst. A chemical reaction takes place which causes hardening (polymerisation) to 'glue' together any cracks. The Wass Research Group says that this can give up to 100 per cent recovery of mechanical strength.Professor Wass was interviewed in an exclusive by the Independent on Sunday. In the interview he said he expected self-healing products to reach consumers in the “very near future” and said that inspiration came from the body's ability to heal itself by forming scabs.
metadata.Further information: BRISTOL has long been at the centre research into the ground-breaking materials that are being used to build the aeroplanes of the future. The work taking place at the National Composite Centre is leading the world and changing the face of the aviation industry. But now a team of scientists from Bristol University has gone one step further and come up with a miraculous compound that can actually heal itself. And if the new technology works not only will it help improve safety in aviation it could also be used in hundreds of different products from nail varnish to safety helmets. The principles are based along the same lines as the way the human body heals itself through blood clotting. The research is being unveiled for the first time at a Royal Society Meeting in London and has already been hailed as a major step forward for manufacturing. The team's ground-breaking work started "on the back of an envelope" but has now got to the stage where it has become usable technology. As well as working for aeroplane fuselages it could also be used to improve nail polish, golf clubs, tennis racquets, fishing rods, bike helmets and even cracked mobile phone screens. The cosmetics giant L'Oréal has contacted the scientists to register its interest. The team has been working on the project for the last three years and even they say it is close to science fiction. The work is so far advanced that the team has been able to produce a set of wings. Professor Duncan Wass, who is leading the research, said there are high hopes that airlines will be able to purchase self-healing products in the 'very near future'. The researchers have been working with aerospace engineers in nearby Filton to look at ways to prevent tiny cracks forming in an aircraft's wings and fuselage. Professor Wass said: "We took inspiration from the human body. We have not evolved to withstand any damage – if we were like that we would have a skin as thick as a rhinoceros – but if we do get damaged, we bleed, and it scabs and heals. "We just put that same sort of function into a synthetic material: let's have something that can heal itself." He added: "We are definitely getting to the stage where in the next five or 10 years we are going to see things like mobile phone screens that can heal themselves if they crack." The healing material can take anywhere between a couple of hours and a day to recover with the process taking place faster in warmer climates. The research is being presented for the first time in public at a conference called Catalysis Improving Society. Professor Wass said: "We are definitely getting to the stage where in the next five or 10 years we're going to see things like mobile phone screens that can heal themselves if they crack." Self-healing technology first emerged in 2001, when researchers at the University of Illinois in the US created a plastic which could repair itself. The same team followed that up in 2014 by creating a polymer which could fix holes of up to three centimetres. As well as help to save lives the technology will also help make safety checks by airlines become much cheaper to carry out. Airbus had to pay out billions when its superjumbo the A380 developed tiny cracks in its wings three years ago. The problem eventually cost the plane manufacturer £120 million to correct. Read more: http://www.bristolpost.co.uk/Self-healing-material-invented-Bristol-scientists/story-26657204-detail/story.html#ixzz40t9fuYHI Follow us: @BristolPost on Twitter | bristolpost on Facebook --------------------------------------------------------------------------- Scientists have developed aircraft wings that can detect and repair small-scale damage to their structure. Professor Duncan Wass, from Bristol University, presented the research, funded by the Engineering and Physical Sciences Research Council (EPSRC), at a scientific meeting organised by the UK's Catalysis Hub. The event at the Royal Society highlighted the latest research into catalysis and how it can improve society with applications for energy and the environment. The UK's Catalysis Hub is funded by EPSRC with catalysis science supporting UK economic growth. How the technology works: Modern aircraft are made with carbon fibre-reinforced composites. These are high performance, lightweight and stiff making them an ideal material for aeroplanes or wind turbines. However, damage to the composite structure can be difficult to detect. The researchers added microcapsules to the composite. If the aircraft wing is damaged these microcapsules rupture and come into contact with a catalyst. A chemical reaction takes place which causes hardening (polymerisation) to 'glue' together any cracks. The Wass Research Group says that this can give up to 100 per cent recovery of mechanical strength.Professor Wass was interviewed in an exclusive by the Independent on Sunday. In the interview he said he expected self-healing products to reach consumers in the “very near future” and said that inspiration came from the body's ability to heal itself by forming scabs. Prof Duncan Wass writes: Fibre-reinforced composites are the modern materials of choice where high performance must be combined with low weight, such as aerospace structures (aeroplanes, wind turbines). However, impact damage to composite structures can be difficult to detect but result in a drastic reduction in mechanical properties. We are adopting a bio-inspired approach to effect damage detection and self-healing. This is a collaborative area of research with Ian Bond and Richard Trask in the Department of Aerospace Engineering, within the ACCIS composites research group. We are providing novel damage detection and self-healing chemistries, to combine with their ability to manufacture and incorporate multifunctional hollow fibres, microcapsules and vascular networks within both composite laminates and sandwich structures. The essential chemistry relies on catalysts which are ‘triggered’ by damage events to cause the polymerisation of a reservoir of monomer held within the composite structure.
